concepts.title: Natural Image
concepts.one_liner: A natural image is a sample from the extremely small subset of all possible pixel arrays that represent real-world visual scenes.
concepts.content:
A natural image is a specific type of high-dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. The space of all possible images is incredibly large; for example, even $32\times32$ color thumbnails with 8 bits per channel allow for more than $10^{7,398}$ possible combinations. However, most of these possible images consist of random noise. The set of natural images occupies only a very small part of this total space. A typical sample from the set of all possible images consists of pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution, whereas a natural image contains structured visual information.

concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the concept of a natural image is fundamental to computer vision and image processing. It establishes that real-world images are not random but follow specific structural patterns, allowing us to distinguish meaningful visual data from noise and build models that can compress, enhance, or generate realistic scenes.

concepts.title: Visual Worlds
concepts.one_liner: Visual worlds are distinct sets of images characterized by specific visual properties, ranging from synthetic noise to real-world scenes.
concepts.content:
Images can be categorized into different visual worlds, each possessing unique visual characteristics. We can differentiate images as belonging to various worlds—such as white noise, Gabor patches, Mondrian patterns, stars, clouds, line drawings, or computer-generated imagery (CGI)—even if those worlds do not resemble our everyday environment. Defining the exact characteristics that distinguish the set of real images from these other synthetic or abstract visual worlds is a complex task.

(see figure: Different visual worlds, some real, some synthetic. (a) White noise. (b) Gabor patches. (c) Mondrian. (d) Stars. (e) Clouds. (f) Line drawing. (g) Computer graphic imagery (CGI). (h) A real street...)
concepts.motivation_md: By categorizing images into different 'worlds,' researchers can isolate specific visual features and study how human or machine vision systems process different types of structure, from pure randomness to complex 3D geometry.

concepts.title: Telling Noise from Texture

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Distinguishing noise from texture involves determining whether visual randomness is an artifact of the imaging process or a physical property of the scene's surfaces.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Telling noise from surface texture. Which one is which?)

How do we tell noise from texture? One might encounter a scene where an image is corrupted with additive stationary noise, or a scene containing an object textured with a pattern that looks like noise. To distinguish them, we look at how the pattern behaves. Stationary image noise is independent of the content of the scene: it is not affected by object boundaries, it does not deform according to the 3D orientation of surfaces, and its frequency does not change with the distance between the camera and the scene. If such noise were actually part of the physical world, it would require a distribution that perfectly conspires with the observer's viewpoint to appear stationary.

concepts.title: Image Denoising

position.section_title: How Do We Tell Noise from Texture?

concepts.one_liner: Image denoising is the process of automatically removing noise from an image by separating the uncorrupted content from the noise component.
concepts.content: Noise is a process independent from image content, and the human visual system does not perceive it as a physical part of the scene (like paint). Image denoising is the task of automatically removing this noise. This process is equivalent to separating an image into two distinct components: one representing a clean, uncorrupted picture and the other containing only the noise. Statistical image models are often employed to achieve this separation.
concepts.motivation_md: Denoising is essential for improving the quality of images captured in low-light conditions or with low-quality sensors, ensuring that subsequent analysis or human viewing is not hindered by artifacts.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoising aims to decompose a noisy image into a clean image and a noise-only component.

key_passage.text: Image denoising consists in removing the noise from an image automatically. This is equivalent to being able to separate the image into two components, one looking like a clean uncorrupted picture and the second image containing only noise.

motivation.text: One important task in image processing is image denoising. Noise is an independent process from the image content, and our visual system does not perceive noise as a strange form of paint.

concepts.title: Independent Pixel Model
concepts.one_liner: The independent pixel model assumes that every pixel's intensity is drawn independently from a single stationary distribution.
concepts.content:
The simplest image model assumes that all pixels are independent and their intensity values are drawn from a stationary distribution, meaning the distribution is independent of the pixel's location. The probability $p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell)$ of an image $\ell[n,m]$ of size $N \times M$ is given by:

$$p_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{m=1}^{M} p_{\theta}\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$$

Here, $\theta$ represents the parameters of the model, which can be fitted to data using maximum likelihood. For a discrete gray-scale image with 256 levels, $\theta$ is a vector of 256 probabilities (a histogram). For color images, it involves $256^3$ bins. 

(see figure: Fitting a statistical image model to a set of training images. Once the model is learned we can use the model to sample new images.)

To assess the model, one can sample new images from it. In a multinomial model, the probability of a pixel at $(n,m)$ having value $k$ is $p_{\theta}(\ell [n,m] = k) = \theta_k$. While this model can somewhat approximate images of stars, it fails to reproduce the structure of most other visual worlds because treating pixels as independent observations ignores the inherent spatial correlations in natural images.

(see figure: Estimation of the image model parameters using one image, and then sampling a new image by sampling pixels independently using the histogram of the training image.)

(see figure: Examples of images and corresponding random samples with the same distribution of pixel intensities. Only the image with stars (a) has some visual similarity with the randomly sampled image.)
concepts.motivation_md: This model serves as a baseline in statistical image processing. While it fails to capture spatial structure, it introduces the concept of using probability distributions and histograms to characterize image content.
concepts.recap_md: - The model treats an image as a collection of independent random variables.

The failure of color histograms as a generative model of images should not be surprising as treating pixels as independent observations is clearly not how images work.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching is a pixelwise transformation that adjusts one image's intensity distribution to match that of another image.
concepts.content:
Histogram matching is a useful operation where, given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$ with histograms $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2$, we seek a pixelwise transformation $f\left(\ell[n,m] \right)$ such that the histogram of the transformed image $f\left(\ell_1 [n,m] \right)$ matches $\mathbf{h}_2$. A common choice is a transformation that preserves the relative ordering of pixel intensities.

This technique has significant perceptual importance. For example, by swapping the histograms of two spheres rendered under different illumination models (such as a campus photograph versus pink noise), the perceived material of the sphere can be transformed from shiny to matte. This demonstrates that simple histogram manipulations can fundamentally change the perception of surface gloss and material properties.

(see figure: Perceptual importance of simple histogram manipulations. Figure from @Fleming2001)
concepts.motivation_md: Histogram matching is used for color correction, normalizing images taken under different lighting conditions, and artistic style transfer by forcing the tonal distribution of one image onto another.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a pixelwise function to align the intensity distributions of two images.

key_passage.text: Given two images ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ with histograms h₁ and h₂, we look for a pixelwise transformation f(ℓ[n,m]) so that the histogram of the transformed image, f(ℓ₁[n,m]), matches the histogram of ℓ₂. There are many ways in which histograms can be transformed. One natural choice is a transformation that preserves the ordering of pixels intensities.

concepts.title: Pink Noise
concepts.one_liner: Pink noise is random noise characterized by a power spectrum that is inversely proportional to the sum of the squared spatial frequencies.
concepts.content: Pink noise is a type of random noise defined by its power spectrum. Specifically, it has a $\frac{1}{|w_x^2+w_y^2|}$ power spectrum, where $w_x$ and $w_y$ represent the spatial frequencies. It is often used in visual experiments and rendering to simulate certain types of naturalistic but random textures.
concepts.motivation_md: Pink noise is frequently used in image processing and vision science because its statistical properties more closely resemble the spatial frequency distributions found in natural scenes compared to white noise.

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF)

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: A Markov random field is an image model where a pixel's probability distribution is independent of other pixels given a sufficient neighborhood of surrounding pixels.
concepts.content: A powerful class of image models is known as Markov random field (MRF) models. The core intuition for these models is that if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. To fit and sample from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models. This Markov structure can be exploited for texture synthesis, based on the intuition that conditioning on a large enough region of nearby pixels effectively determines the value of the central pixel. This same intuition can be applied to the problem of image denoising.
concepts.motivation_md: MRF models provide a way to capture local spatial dependencies in images. By assuming that a pixel only depends on its immediate neighbors, we can simplify complex global image distributions into manageable local interactions, which is essential for tasks like denoising and texture synthesis.
concepts.recap_md: - A pixel's value is conditionally independent of the rest of the image given its neighbors.

concepts.title: Nonlocal Means Denoising

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

concepts.one_liner: Nonlocal means denoising computes a pixel's value as a weighted sum of all other pixels, where weights depend on the similarity of their local neighborhoods.
concepts.content:
The nonlocal means denoising algorithm defines the denoised image as a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels. More formally,
$$\ell_{\mbox{NLM}}[n,m] = \sum_{k,l} w_{n,m}[k,l] \ell[k,l]$$ where
$$w_{n,m}[k,l] = \frac{1}{Z_{n,m}} \exp{\frac{- \left| \ell[N_{k,l}] - ℓ[N_{n,m}] \right| ^2}{h^2}},$$
where $N_{i, j}$ denotes an $h \times h$ region of pixels centered at $i, j$, and $Z_{n,m}$ is a normalization constant such that $\sum_{kl} w_{n,m}[k,l] = 1$.

[FIGURE:c5b8102b308188df | Regions of support for the nonlocal means denoising algorithm. Source: Image from @Baudes2005]

The parameter $h$ is typically set to $10 \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the estimated image noise standard deviation. The weighting function $w_{n,m}[k,l]$ indicates which pixels are averaged together to yield the nonlocal mean value; the algorithm effectively samples from image regions with similar local structure to the position being denoised.

(see figure: Nonlocal means denoising algorithm results. (left) Original image without noise. (middle) Noisy image. (right) Denoised image.Source:Figure from @Baudes2011)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional denoising filters often blur edges by averaging nearby pixels regardless of content. Nonlocal means improves this by averaging pixels that have similar surrounding patterns, even if they are far apart in the image, preserving repetitive structures and textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoising is achieved by a weighted average of pixels based on neighborhood similarity.

concepts.title: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate
concepts.one_liner: The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value that maximizes the posterior density $p(\boldsymbol\ell | \boldsymbol\ell_g)$ to recover an uncorrupted image.
concepts.content:
The maximum a posteriori, or MAP, estimate $\boldsymbol\ell_g$ of an uncorrupted image is defined by maximizing the posterior density:
$$\max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p(\boldsymbol\ell\bigm | \boldsymbol\ell_g)$$
In these equations, the image is represented as a column vector $\boldsymbol\ell$. This posterior density can be rewritten using Bayes' rule as:
$$\max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p({\boldsymbol\ell} \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}_g) = \max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) p({\boldsymbol\ell})$$
concepts.motivation_md: In image restoration, we often have a corrupted observation and need a principled way to guess the original image. The MAP estimate provides a statistical framework to combine observed data with prior knowledge about what natural images look like.
concepts.recap_md: - The MAP estimate finds the most probable original image given the observed corrupted data.

concepts.title: Wavelet marginal model
concepts.one_liner: The wavelet marginal model extends Gaussian priors by using localized filters and measuring the histogram shape of filter responses to capture local image structures.
concepts.content: The wavelet marginal model extends the standard Gaussian prior model to better capture important image properties such as flat regions, edges, and lines. While Gaussian models capture correlations that decrease with distance, they often fail to represent local structures. This model improves upon them in two ways: (1) it uses localized filters instead of sinusoids that span the entire image, helping to capture local structures like lines and edges; and (2) instead of characterizing filter outputs by a single number like mean power, it measures the histogram shape of all filter responses.
concepts.motivation_md: Gaussian priors tend to generate cloud-like images because they only capture basic correlations. To represent natural images with sharp features like edges and flat regions, we need a model that accounts for the specific local statistics of filter responses.

concepts.title: Non-Gaussian distribution of image derivatives
concepts.one_liner: Natural images filtered with band-pass filters exhibit highly non-Gaussian distributions characterized by a sharp peak at zero and heavy tails.
concepts.content:
When filtering images with band-pass filters, such as image derivatives or Gabor filters, the output has a remarkably non-Gaussian distribution. (see figure: (a) Input image. (b) Horizontal and (c) vertical derivatives of the input image. (d) Histogram of pixel intensities of the input image. (e and f) Histograms of the two derivatives of the original...)

While the histogram of an unfiltered image is also non-Gaussian, it lacks a consistent structure across different images. In contrast, the histograms of filter outputs like $\left[-1,1\right]$ and $\left[-1,1\right]^\mathsf{T}$ are very clean, symmetric, and have a unique maximum around zero. This behavior contradicts the Gaussian image model hypothesis; if an image were truly Gaussian, any linear operation like filtering would also result in a Gaussian distribution. Band-pass filtered Gaussian noise is still Gaussian...)

concepts.title: Generalized Laplacian distribution
concepts.one_liner: The generalized Laplacian distribution is a two-parameter function that accurately models the non-Gaussian statistics of band-pass filtered natural images.
concepts.content:
The distribution of intensity values in an image filtered by a band-pass filter $h$, denoted $\boldsymbol\ell_h = \boldsymbol\ell\circ \mathbf{h}$, can be parameterized by the generalized Laplacian distribution:
$$p(\ell_h[n,m] = x) = \frac{\exp \left(- \left| x/s  \right|^r \right)}{2 (s/r) \Gamma(1/r)}$$
This distribution has two parameters: the exponent $r$, which alters the shape, and the scale parameter $s$, which influences variance. In natural images, $r$ typically lies within the range $[0.4, 0.8]$. 

(see figure: Generalized Laplacian distribution with $s=1$ and (a) $r=0.1$, (b) $r=1$, (c) $r=2$, and (d) $r=10$. %Changing the exponent $r$ changes the shape of the distribution, generating some special case...)

Different values of $r$ yield familiar distributions: $r=2$ is Gaussian, $r=1$ is the standard Laplacian, $r \to \infty$ is a uniform distribution, and $r \to 0$ converges to a delta function.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard Gaussian distributions fail to model the 'heavy tails' and sharp peaks seen in image derivatives. The generalized Laplacian provides a flexible mathematical form that can fit these empirical observations by adjusting the shape parameter $r$.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameterized by shape $r$ and scale $s$, fitting natural image filter outputs well.

concepts.title: Wavelet marginal prior model
concepts.one_liner: The wavelet marginal prior model defines the probability of an image as the product of the probabilities of its individual filter responses.
concepts.content:
To capture the statistical properties of natural images, we can define a prior model based on a filter bank of $K$ kernels $h_k [n,m]$. This bank may include Gaussian derivatives, Gabor filters, or steerable filters. Assuming the output of each filter is independent, the prior model for natural images is expressed as:
$$p(\boldsymbol\ell) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} \prod_{n,m} p_k(\ell_k [n,m])$$
This distribution represents the product over all filters and locations of the likelihood of each filtered value, where each $p_k$ follows the generalized Laplacian distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: By formalizing the observed statistics of image derivatives into a joint probability distribution, we create a mathematical 'prior' that can be used to solve inverse problems like denoising or inpainting.
concepts.recap_md: - Models the image prior as a product of independent filter response distributions.

concepts.title: Bayesian Image Denoising
concepts.one_liner: Bayesian image denoising uses the Laplacian prior of subband coefficients and a Gaussian likelihood to calculate the most probable denoised values.
concepts.content:
Bayesian image denoising leverages the highly kurtotic distribution of band-pass filter responses. Assuming zero-mean additive Gaussian noise with variance $\sigma^2$, the likelihood of a true coefficient value $x$ given an observed noisy coefficient $\hat{x}$ is:
$$p(\hat{x} \bigm | x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - ̂{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$
The prior probability $p(x)$ is modeled as a Laplacian distribution ($r=1$):
$$p(x) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right) }$$
By Bayes' rule, the posterior probability is the product of these two:
$$P(x \bigm | \hat{x}) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right)} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - \hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }$$
(see figure: Showing the likelihood, prior, and posterior terms for the estimation of a subband coefficient from several noisy observations. (a) A zero subband coefficient is observed. (b) An observation of 0.26...)
This approach leads to a MAP estimate that can be implemented via a coring function, where observed coefficients near zero are suppressed. (see figure: Input/output coring curve for maximum posterior denoising for the example of @fig-waveletBayes)
concepts.motivation_md: Simple averaging filters blur edges. Bayesian denoising using wavelet priors allows us to distinguish between actual image structure (which is sparse and high-amplitude) and noise (which is Gaussian), preserving edges while removing grain.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines a Gaussian noise likelihood with a Laplacian image prior using Bayes' rule.

key_passage.text: By Bayes rule, the posterior probability is the product of those two functions, P(x | \hat{x}) \propto \exp{ \left( -\frac{\left| x \right|}{s} \right)} \exp{ \left( -\frac{(x - \hat{x})^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) }. This implements a coring function: if a coefficient value is observed near zero, it is set to zero, based on the very high prior probability of zero coefficient values.

concepts.title: Pixel correlation in natural images
concepts.one_liner: The intensities of nearby pixels in natural images are highly correlated, with correlation values that slowly decay as the distance between pixels increases.
concepts.content: In the quest to find what makes photographs of everyday scenes special, the next simplest image structure is a set of two pixels. If one plots the value of the intensity of one pixel as a function of the intensity value of the pixel nearby, the scatterplot produced by many pixel pairs (see figure: (center) Scatter plots of pairs of pixels intensities as a function of distance and (right) cross-correlation as a function for vertical (green) and horizontal (red) displacements for the street...) is concentrated on the identity line. As we look at the correlation between pixels that are farther away, the correlation value slowly decays. The correlation, $C$, between two pixels separated by offsets of $\Delta n$ and $\Delta m$, is: $$C(\Delta n, \Delta m) = \rho \left( \ell[n+\Delta n,m+ \Delta m], \ell[n,m] \right)$$ where $$\rho \left( a, b \right) = \frac{E \left( (a-\bar{a})( b- \bar{b}) \right)}{\sigma_a \sigma_b},$$ where $\sigma_a$ is the standard deviation of the variable $a$, and $\bar{a}$ is the mean of $a$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the statistical relationship between neighboring pixels is the first step in characterizing the structure of natural images, distinguishing them from purely random noise.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nearby pixels in natural images exhibit high intensity correlation, appearing concentrated on the identity line in scatterplots.
 - The correlation value $C$ decays as the spatial offset $(\Delta n, \Delta m)$ between pixels increases.
 - Correlation is mathematically defined using the Pearson correlation coefficient $\rho$ between pixel intensities.

concepts.title: Power spectrum of natural images
concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the 2D Fourier transform of most natural images falls off as a power law $1/w^\alpha$ with $\alpha \simeq 1$.
concepts.content:
The correlation function is related to the magnitude of the Fourier transform of an image. The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation of a signal is the square of magnitude of its Fourier Transform, $\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert ^2$, which is the power spectrum of a signal. One remarkable property of most natural images is that if you take the 2D Fourier transform of an image, its magnitude falls off as a power law in frequency: $$\lVert \mathscr{L}(u,v) \rVert \simeq \frac{1}{ w ^ \alpha}$$ where $w$ denotes the radial spatial frequency ($w = \sqrt{u + v}$), $\mathscr{L}(u,v)$ is the Fourier transform of the image $\ell[n,m]$, and $\alpha \simeq 1$. This is true for all orientations. 

(see figure: (top) Three natural images with size 512 $\times$ 512 pixels, and one random image. (middle) The magnitude of their Fourier transforms (FT), images are transformed to grayscale by averaging the three...) 

As seen in , the largest amplitudes concentrate in the low spatial frequencies for natural images, whereas random images have similar spectral content at all frequencies. When expressing the FT in polar coordinates and calculating the average magnitude over all angular directions, the decay along the radial frequency roughly follows a $1/w^{1.5}$ decay in many examples, a property shared across distinct natural images.
concepts.motivation_md: The $1/w^\alpha$ power law is a fundamental statistical regularity of natural scenes that has influenced the evolution of biological visual systems and the design of image processing algorithms.
concepts.recap_md:
- Natural images exhibit a power spectrum where magnitude decreases as frequency increases, following $1/w^\alpha$.
 - Unlike natural images, white noise (random images) has a flat power spectrum with similar content at all frequencies.
 - This spectral decay is generally consistent across different orientations and image contents.

concepts.title: Gaussian image model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian image model is a maximum entropy statistical model that accounts for pixel correlations and the power law spectrum of natural images.
concepts.content: The Gaussian model is a statistical image model that takes into account the correlation statistics and the power spectrum of natural images. If the only constraint we have is the correlation function among image pixels, the maximum entropy distribution is the Gaussian distribution: $$p(\boldsymbol\ell) \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol\ell^\mathsf{T}{\bf C}^{-1} \boldsymbol\ell\right)$$ where ${\bf C}$ is the covariance matrix of all the image pixels. This model accounts for the correlation of intensity values between different pixels. For stationary signals, the covariance matrix ${\bf C}$ has a circulant structure and can be diagonalized using the Fourier transform: ${\bf C} = {\bf F}{\bf D}{\bf F}^\mathsf{T}$. concepts.title: Sampling with PCA decorrelation
concepts.one_liner: PCA decorrelation allows for sampling new images that maintain the color distribution of an input image by processing decorrelated color channels independently.
concepts.content: We can sample new images by matching the parameters of individual natural images. To process color images, we first look for a color space that decorrelates color information for each image. This is done by applying principal component analysis (PCA) to the three color channels, resulting in a $3 \times 3$ matrix that produces three decorrelated channels. concepts.title: Limitations of the Gaussian image model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian image model generally produces cloud-like noise because it fails to capture the structural properties that make natural images look real.
concepts.content: As shown in , when fitting the Gaussian model to different real images and sampling from it, the result is always an image that looks like cloudy noise regardless of the image content. However, a few attributes of the original image are preserved, including the size of details and dominant orientations.   Fig (a) Photograph of hair. (b) Random draw of Gaussian image model using covariance matrix fit from (a). For this unusual image, the model works well because the input is mostly one-dimensional (1D), with variations occurring across one orientation and remaining constant along the perpendicular direction. This specific structure can be captured by the magnitude of the Fourier transform, but this is an exception for the Gaussian image model.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying where the Gaussian model fails (e.g., failing to represent edges and shapes) motivates the development of more complex, non-Gaussian statistical models.
concepts.recap_md:

concepts.title: Image denoising with Wiener filter
concepts.one_liner: The Wiener filter performs image denoising by finding the maximum a posteriori estimate of an image under a Gaussian prior and additive white Gaussian noise.
concepts.content: Image denoising can be performed using the prior on the structure of the correlation of natural images. In this problem, we observe a noisy image $\boldsymbol\ell_g$ corrupted with white Gaussian noise: $$\ell_g[n, m] = \ell[n, m] + g[n, m]$$ The goal is to recover the uncorrupted image $\ell[n,m]$ by finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate: $\max_{\boldsymbol\ell} p(\boldsymbol\ell\bigm | \boldsymbol\ell_g)$. This posterior density is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior: $p({\boldsymbol\ell}_g \bigm | {\boldsymbol\ell}) \propto \exp( - \left| {\boldsymbol\ell}_g - {\boldsymbol\ell} \right| ^2 / \sigma_g^2)$ and $p({\boldsymbol\ell}) \propto \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} {\boldsymbol\ell}^T {\bf C}^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell} \right)$. The solution is a linear operation: $${\boldsymbol\ell} = {\bf C} \left( {\bf C} + \sigma_g^2 \mathbf{I} \right)^{-1} {\boldsymbol\ell}_g$$ In the Fourier domain, this is: $$\mathscr{L}(v) = \frac{A/|v|^{2\alpha}}{A/|v|^{2\alpha} + \sigma_g^2} \mathscr{L}_g(v)$$ (see figure: (Top row) Ground truth decomposition of image into Gaussian white noise and the image, uncorrupted by noise. (bottom row) Gaussian image model denoising results. Note that the estimated noise image...) Although there is some noise reduction, the result is often unsatisfactory because the Gaussian model fails to capture the properties that make a natural image look real.
concepts.motivation_md: The Wiener filter provides an optimal linear solution for denoising when the signal and noise statistics are known, serving as a baseline for more advanced image restoration techniques.
concepts.recap_md:
- Denoising is formulated as a MAP estimation problem combining a Gaussian likelihood and a Gaussian prior.
 - The resulting filter is a linear operation that can be efficiently implemented in the Fourier domain.
 - While it reduces noise, the output often lacks the sharpness and structure of real natural images.
